questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Extracts with no majority code
questions.learningObjective: Decide how to handle extracts that no analyst codes consistently.
questions.stem: Marta Beaulieu codes every line of her club interviews, yet seven lines about telescope setup have no single code a second analyst would choose.

options.text: She should give each of those lines the code used most often in the surrounding talk.
options.misconception: Believes every line needs a code and blanks signal sloppy work.

options.text: She should delete those seven lines so the code counts describe only clear material.
options.misconception: Thinks discarding off-topic lines cleans the analysis.

options.text: She should keep the lines under an uncertainty code and report them separately.
She should have both analysts vote on each line until one code wins a majority.
options.misconception: Believes majority voting settles real ambiguity.

questions.explanation: Lines that no analyst codes alike show genuine ambiguity in the material rather than careless coding. Marking them with a distinct uncertainty code keeps that evidence visible instead of forcing a meaning the coders do not share.
questions.hint: Ambiguous material is a finding, not a gap to be filled.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: New codes per interview after the plateau
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a flat run of new-code counts in a coding sequence.
questions.stem: Tomas Reyes codes his interviews in sequence and the new-code counts run 7, 5, 4, 2, 1, 0, 0, 0 across eight interviews.

options.text: The codebook stopped changing after interview five, which is the pattern saturation names.
The sample was oversized, so the final three interviews should be removed from the study.
options.misconception: Reads a plateau as proof the sample was too large.

options.text: The later interviews were redundant and carry no information worth keeping.
options.misconception: Believes redundant interviews have no analytic value.

options.text: The topic is exhausted, so no later study of club observing is ever justified.
options.misconception: Treats a coding plateau as proof the topic is closed.

questions.explanation: Interviews that add no new codes show the codebook has stopped changing, the signal behind saturation. A plateau does not mean the sample was oversized, that later interviews lack value, or that the topic is closed for good.
questions.hint: A plateau describes codebook stability, not sample size.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Coverage of a joint display
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a joint display shows about analytic coverage.
questions.stem: Ada Nkemelu crosses nine analytic codes against fourteen interviewees in a joint display and must explain why some rows are thin.

answer.exemplar: A joint display puts codes in rows and interviewees in columns, so coverage becomes visible: which codes recur across many interviews, which appear in only a few, and which cells stay empty. Thin rows are not automatically a defect. They mark codes that may be genuinely rare, may belong to a particular subgroup, or may need sharper specification before another round of coding, and saying so keeps the display a diagnostic rather than a results table.

questions.explanation: A joint display makes coverage visible by showing which codes pair with which interviewees. Thin rows prompt a look at specification or subgroup, they are not defects to hide or findings to over-read.
questions.hint: Coverage means how codes spread across participants, not volume.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Counting theme instances at the unit of analysis
questions.learningObjective: Compute interview-level counts of a theme across two logging periods.
questions.stem: Hal Wendt finds the theme first light anxiety in 7 of his 12 interviews and 11 of his partner's 14 interviews. How many of the combined 26 interviews contain no instance of the theme?
questions.explanation: The two logs hold 12 plus 14, or 26, interviews, and 7 plus 11, or 18, of them carry the theme. Removing those 18 leaves 8 interviews with no instance of it.
questions.hint: Count the interviews that lack the theme, not its instances.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Chance-corrected agreement with lopsided margins
questions.learningObjective: Choose a defensible way to report agreement when one code dominates.
questions.stem: Priya Raghunathan has two coders on a codebook that places 88 percent of excerpts in a single code and asks how their agreement should be reported.

options.text: Report raw agreement only, because any correction would merely confuse readers of the log.
options.misconception: Thinks raw agreement is enough when one code dominates.

options.text: Report a chance-corrected statistic alongside the code frequencies, since chance agreement is high here.
Report the corrected coefficient alone and drop the frequencies, which are only background detail.
options.misconception: Believes base rates need not be shown to readers.

options.text: Report the single most contested excerpt, since one hard case settles the quality of the coding.
options.misconception: Believes one disputed excerpt determines the coefficient.

questions.explanation: With most excerpts in one code, coders agree by chance often, so raw agreement flatters them. A chance-corrected statistic shows agreement above that baseline, and base rates belong in the report.
questions.hint: A dominant code inflates raw agreement, so correct for chance.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a saturation claim commits you to
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the reporting steps that a saturation claim requires.
questions.stem: Jun-seo Pak must lay out what his saturation claim obliges the paper to report; choose the most defensible order of steps.

options.text: State the conditions under which a new case would force the claims to be revised.
options.misconception: Treats the boundary of a claim as a closing formality.

options.text: Show how the pattern of new codes changed across successive interviews.
options.misconception: Presents the new-code pattern as a decorative extra.

options.text: State the sampling frame and how the participating observers were chosen.
options.misconception: Treats sampling as background detail behind the claim.

options.text: Document which coding decisions changed as the analysis proceeded.
options.misconception: Assumes the codebook was fixed from the first interview.

questions.explanation: A saturation claim is a claim about data collection, so sampling comes first, then the coding decisions, then the new-code pattern showing the codebook stabilised, and finally the boundary conditions of the claim.
questions.hint: Sampling, then coding, then evidence, then limits of the claim.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a transferability claim rests on
questions.learningObjective: Select the basis on which findings can travel to another setting.
questions.stem: Elena Sokolova knows one branch of amateur astronomers well and wants her findings to travel to branches she has never visited.

options.text: She should widen her sample to every region before claiming the findings travel anywhere.
options.misconception: Believes sample size is the only basis for transferability.

options.text: She should describe her participants and setting closely enough that readers can judge fit.
She should state that the findings hold everywhere because two analysts agreed on the codes.
options.misconception: Believes local replication makes findings universal.

options.text: She should strip out site-specific detail so the findings look portable on their face.
options.misconception: Thinks removing context makes findings travel further.

questions.explanation: Transferability rests on a thick description of participants and setting, so readers can judge how far findings travel. Sample size, replication at one site, and stripped context each fail to support portability.
questions.hint: Transferability is a judgement a reader makes from description.

questions.stem: Marcus Ibe counts the code cloudless hour 27 times across 9 interviews, and two of those interviews hold six instances each.

options.text: Two interviews carry most of the instances, so the analysis should start from them.
options.misconception: Assumes many instances means few people hold the theme.

options.text: Most interviews contribute one or two instances, so the theme is widely shared but thin.
Twenty-seven instances across nine interviews is too much material for one code.
options.misconception: Judges a theme by raw instance count alone.

options.text: The unit of analysis should be the instance rather than the interview.
options.misconception: Assumes instances can stand in for interviews as units.

questions.explanation: Twenty-seven instances across nine interviews, with two interviews holding six each, means most interviews contribute one or two. The theme is broad but shallow, and the unit of analysis must match the claim.
questions.hint: A few dense interviews do not make a theme a minority one.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Chance-corrected agreement with lopsided margins
questions.learningObjective: Order the steps needed to produce a corrected agreement coefficient.
questions.stem: Ruth Delacroix wants the base rate her two coders share before she can compute a corrected agreement figure; which pairing of numbers answers both steps in order?

options.text: Chance-expected agreement from the code margins first, then the corrected coefficient from it.
The corrected coefficient from raw agreement first, with the base rate added afterwards.
options.misconception: Corrects before establishing the base rate.

options.text: The code margins alone, since they already contain the whole agreement result.
options.misconception: Believes base rates capture the full agreement picture.

options.text: The number of codes in the codebook first, since counts are what the correction needs.
options.misconception: Thinks the correction is computed from code counts.

questions.explanation: Chance-corrected agreement needs the base rate first, since the correction depends on how codes are distributed, then the observed agreement. Reversing the order leaves the coefficient without its baseline.
questions.hint: Establish what chance alone would produce before correcting.

questions.topic: New codes per interview after the plateau
questions.learningObjective: Read a coding record that shows new-code counts over successive interviews.

stimulus.body: Three lines from the branch bulletin: interview nine settled the argument about the new focuser and added nothing further. Interview ten raised the cost of batteries and the winter guest list. Interview eleven repeated the guest list and added nothing.

questions.stem: Sam Okonkwo reads the bulletin as a coding record and asks what the pattern of new codes per interview supports.

options.text: The coding stalled because the interviewer stopped asking about unfamiliar ground.
options.misconception: Blames the plateau on the interviewer rather than the data.

options.text: The sample should be doubled to be sure the plateau is genuine.
options.misconception: Treats a plateau as a sample size problem.

options.text: Coding has stabilised, so later interviews test the codebook rather than change it.
The last two interviews should be dropped for breaking the codebook rules.
options.misconception: Treats a stable codebook as grounds for discarding data.

questions.explanation: Two interviews in a row adding no new codes is the pattern a saturation claim rests on. It does not show the interviewer went stale, that more interviews are needed, or that recent data broke the rules.
questions.hint: A run of zeroes is evidence about the codebook, not about the interviewer.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a saturation claim commits you to
questions.learningObjective: State the evidentiary obligations created by a saturation claim.
questions.stem: Nils Brandt plans to write that his interview study of club observing reached saturation and asks what that sentence commits him to show.

answer.exemplar: A saturation claim obliges the author to show how the sample was generated, what coding decisions changed along the way, and the pattern of new themes across interviews, so a reader can see that the codebook stopped changing instead of taking it on trust. It also obliges the author to name the boundary of the claim: for whom, in what setting, and under what conditions a new case would force the account to be rewritten.

questions.explanation: A saturation claim is about data collection, so show sampling, coding decisions, and the new-theme pattern. Otherwise no reader can check it, and you must say where the claim holds.
questions.hint: A claim about sampling has to be visible in the sampling.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Chance-corrected agreement with lopsided margins
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a chance-corrected agreement coefficient from observed and expected agreement.
questions.stem: Two coders sort 100 excerpts and agree on 86 of them, while the chance-expected agreement for their code distribution is 0.44. What is the chance-corrected agreement coefficient?
questions.explanation: Subtract chance from observed and divide by the remaining headroom: 0.86 minus 0.44 is 0.42, and 1 minus 0.44 is 0.56, so 0.42 over 0.56 is 0.75.
questions.hint: Subtract chance agreement, then divide by what is left.

options.text: That the findings have been tested in a second, unrelated club.
options.misconception: Confuses saturation with replication elsewhere.

That the coding scheme was fixed before a single interview was conducted.

questions.hint: Saturation is about change in the codebook, not coverage of the world.

questions.topic: Extracts with no majority code
questions.learningObjective: Respond to coder disagreement that points at the code definitions.
questions.stem: Ines Alvarado finds that two coders each chose different codes for four extracts about dew on the mirror.

options.text: She should pick one of the two codes per extract and continue without comment.
options.misconception: Hides the disagreement instead of revising definitions.

options.text: She should record the disagreement and refine the code definitions it exposes.
She should drop the four extracts because no two coders could agree.
options.misconception: Treats disagreement as grounds for deleting data.

options.text: She should add a fifth code to capture the sort of extract involved.
options.misconception: Adds codes instead of sharpening existing ones.

questions.explanation: Disagreement about which code applies usually means two code definitions overlap, so the fix is a sharper definition rather than a deletion or a new code. Recording the disagreement is what makes the revision visible.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a codebook plateau from a feeling of completeness.

options.text: When the number of interviews matches the number of codes in the codebook.
options.misconception: Believes counts should match for saturation.

When the last member of the branch has been interviewed.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Counting theme instances at the unit of analysis
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the unit of analysis determines what a count means.
questions.stem: Omar Haddad must explain to his club why his report counts interviews rather than raw instances of each theme.

answer.exemplar: The unit of analysis sets what the counts mean. If the claim is about what members experienced, then the interview is the unit and the report says how many interviewees carried the theme, not how many times the phrase appeared. Counting instances instead inflates the apparent weight of a few articulate members, because one person who repeats a phrase three times would otherwise count as three pieces of evidence for a theme the rest of the club barely raised.

questions.explanation: Counting instances lets one talkative member inflate a theme, so instance totals answer a different question than the study's claim. Fixing the interview as the unit counts each member once.
questions.hint: Match the unit to the claim you are making.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Chance-corrected agreement with lopsided margins
questions.learningObjective: Compute the chance-expected agreement from two code distributions.
questions.stem: Tove Andersen codes 100 excerpts. One coder places 84 excerpts in the code clear sky and the other places 70 there. What is the chance-expected agreement for their code distributions?
questions.explanation: Expected agreement is the product of the marginals: 0.84 times 0.70 is 0.588, and 0.16 times 0.30 is 0.048, so the expected share is 0.588 plus 0.048, which is 0.636.
questions.hint: Expected agreement comes from the two margins multiplied.

questions.stem: Rosa Iglesias wants her findings to be usable by a club she has never visited; choose the order that makes that claim credible.

questions.learningObjective: Decide how to record extracts that no code fits consistently.
questions.stem: Sanne Bakker has 300 coded extracts and finds that nine extracts fit no single code with confidence.

options.misconception: Resolves ambiguity by fiat without recording it.

options.text: She should treat the ambiguity as information about the extracts and record the decision.

options.misconception: Treats unclear extracts as removable noise.

questions.learningObjective: Describe what a coder agreement report must contain when one code dominates.
questions.stem: Farida Boussaid reports agreement between two coders on a codebook where most excerpts fall in a single code.

answer.exemplar: The report should give the observed agreement, the agreement expected by chance from the marginal distributions, and the resulting chance-corrected coefficient, with the code frequencies shown alongside. When one code takes most of the material, chance alone produces a high expected agreement, so a raw agreement figure flatters the coders and can suggest a reliability the codebook does not have. The margins are what let a reader judge that for themselves.

questions.explanation: With one dominant code, chance agreement is high and raw agreement overstates reliability. Reporting the base rate and the corrected coefficient lets readers see how much agreement was actually earned.

options.misconception: Judges a scheme from a handful of disagreements.

options.text: They are too few to matter and should not be mentioned in the report.
options.misconception: Treats a small number of disputes as noise to hide.

options.text: They should be dropped, since a coder who cannot decide is not coding properly.
options.misconception: Blames the coder for ambiguous definitions.

options.text: They are a signal to sharpen the code definitions rather than to discard the material.

questions.explanation: Three irreconcilable extracts out of 120 point at definitions that are not yet decidable, which is exactly what a coding round is for. Dropping them or dismissing them as noise leaves the definitions unchanged.

options.text: The study needs at least three more interviews to be certain the plateau is real.
options.misconception: Believes a plateau needs a fixed extra sample.

options.text: The scheme is still changing, because new themes can always be found if you look harder.
options.misconception: Treats the search for themes as endless.

options.text: The codebook settled after interview five, and the later interviews test the settled scheme.
The interviews should be reordered so the new-code counts fall more smoothly.
options.misconception: Believes sequence shapes the plateau.

questions.stem: Rosa Iglesias's joint display shows one code appearing for nine of twelve interviewees and three codes appearing once each.

options.misconception: Removes evidence rather than examining it.

options.text: The display should show only codes that appear for most interviewees.
options.misconception: Filters the display to flatter the findings.

options.misconception: Reports only the code that flatters the account.

options.text: The display makes the pattern visible without deciding whether thin codes are rare or mis-specified.

questions.stem: Nils Brandt finds the theme cloudless hour in all 11 of his interviews; two interviews hold 5 instances each and the other nine hold 21 between them.

options.text: Twenty-one instances spread over nine interviews means most interviews carry three or more.
options.misconception: Guesses per-interview counts from an average.

options.text: The theme reaches every interview, so it is broadly shared even though some dwell on it.

options.misconception: Splits a theme by frequency instead of by meaning.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a saturation claim commits you to
questions.learningObjective: Explain the scope and limits of what a saturation claim licenses.
questions.stem: Sanne Bakker must explain to reviewers what her saturation claim does and does not license her to say.

answer.exemplar: A saturation claim licenses the author to say that the codebook stopped changing under the stated sampling and coding conditions, and it licenses nothing about other clubs, other observers or other periods. It therefore needs the sampling, the coding decisions, and the new-theme pattern shown, plus an explicit statement of the conditions that would reopen the question. Without those, the phrase functions as a claim to authority rather than a reportable finding.

questions.explanation: Saturation speaks to codebook stability under stated conditions and travels poorly beyond them. Show the sampling, the coding decisions and the pattern, and say what would reopen the question.
questions.hint: A claim with limits is stronger than a claim with reach.

options.misconception: Removes the detail that supports the transfer claim.

Draft sharper code definitions for the concepts the extracts reveal.

options.misconception: Adds a marker before deciding what the extracts are about.

options.text: Decide whether the extracts belong to an existing code or need a new one.
options.misconception: Decides the destination before recording the disagreement.

questions.explanation: Document what each analyst chose, then decide whether the extracts fit existing codes or need new ones, then sharpen those definitions, and keep residual uncertainty visible in the counts.

options.text: By stating that the six members agreed with one another on the main themes.
options.misconception: Substitutes member agreement for codebook stability.

options.text: By reporting how many new codes each interview introduced, in sequence.
By describing the final codebook and showing that it covers all six interviews.
options.misconception: Describes coverage instead of change over time.

options.text: By noting that no theme appeared in fewer than two of the six interviews.
options.misconception: Uses a rarity threshold to stand in for a plateau.

questions.explanation: Codebook stability is shown by the number of new codes each interview introduced, read in order. Member agreement, final coverage and rarity thresholds describe other things and cannot show when change stopped.
questions.hint: Stability is a change over time, so report the sequence.

options.text: All sixty cells are filled, because each code has somewhere to go.
options.misconception: Assumes a full grid by default.

options.text: Twenty cells are filled, because only the two broad codes count.
options.misconception: Counts only the codes that are everywhere.

Twelve cells are filled, since only the four narrow codes produce cells.
options.misconception: Ignores the codes present for every interviewee.

options.text: The number of interviews carrying the theme, and the number of interviews in the study.
The number of instances of the theme, and the number of interviews in the study.
options.misconception: Reports instance counts where interview counts belong.

options.text: The number of interviews carrying the theme, and the number of codes in the codebook.
options.misconception: Pairs coverage with codebook size.

options.text: The number of themes in the codebook, and the number of interviews in the study.
options.misconception: Reports category counts rather than theme reach.

questions.explanation: Sharing is expressed as the interviews that carry the theme over the interviews studied. Instance counts answer a different question, and codebook size or theme totals say nothing about spread.

questions.topic: Chance-corrected agreement with lopsided margins
questions.learningObjective: Read a coding record showing where two coders disagree.

stimulus.body: Coding sheet from a club study: excerpt 41 is marked clear sky by one coder and doubtful transparency by the other, and the same pattern recurs across 30 of the 90 excerpts.

questions.stem: Emil Novak reads the coding sheet and asks what the pattern of disagreement implies for the report.

options.text: The coders disagree at random, so averaging their codes removes the problem.
options.misconception: Believes random disagreement cancels out on its own.

options.text: The disagreement concentrates on one codebook boundary, so the definitions need work.
A third coder should settle each disputed excerpt and the record left alone.
options.misconception: Adds a tie-breaker instead of fixing definitions.

options.text: The report should give the raw agreement figure and leave the pattern unremarked.
options.misconception: Reports agreement without noting where it fails.

questions.explanation: Thirty of ninety excerpts turning on the same boundary shows a definitional problem, not random noise. Fixing the definitions is the root repair; averaging or tie-breaking leaves the scheme unchanged.
questions.hint: A pattern in the disagreements points at a definition.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a saturation claim commits you to
questions.learningObjective: Write saturation language a reader can check.
questions.stem: Niamh Carroll wants her paper's language on saturation to be checkable by a reader who never met her.

answer.exemplar: The wording should tie the claim to observable conditions: which participants were sampled, how coding proceeded, and the pattern of new themes across interviews. A reader should be able to look at the new-theme pattern and see the point at which the codebook stopped changing, and to see the boundaries the author placed around the claim. Language such as the study obviously covered everything invites the reader to supply evidence the study never produced, and puts the burden of proof on the reader rather than the author.

questions.explanation: Saturation language should point to observable evidence: sampling, coding, and the new-theme pattern. Otherwise the reader must supply evidence the study never produced.
questions.hint: Write the claim so a stranger can check it.

questions.stem: Yuki Tanabe finds 40 extracts in which two analysts would each pick a different code with equal confidence.

options.text: She should let a third analyst pick the more natural code for each of the forty.
options.misconception: Resolves ambiguity by adding authority, not clarity.

options.text: She should treat the ambiguity as a boundary problem in the codebook and revise the definitions.
She should combine the two codes into one broad code so no choice is needed.
options.misconception: Widens a code to dodge a definitional problem.

options.text: She should exclude the forty extracts because they do not fit the scheme.
options.misconception: Treats awkward material as removable.

questions.explanation: Forty extracts where the choice is genuinely open point at a boundary the codebook has not drawn. Revising the definitions addresses the cause, while a third analyst, a broader code or exclusion each leave the problem in place.

options.text: The codebook settled at interview three, since the counts first reached two.
options.misconception: Calls a plateau at the first repeated value.

options.text: The scheme changed at every interview, because one new code still appears at interview five.
options.misconception: Requires an unbroken run of zeros to claim stability.

options.text: The codebook settled at interview six, since the final two interviews changed nothing.
The counts show the interviews were too long, since more codes appeared in the early ones.
options.misconception: Blames interview length for codebook change.

questions.explanation: The final two interviews both added no codes, so the codebook stopped changing at interview six. A repeated value mid-series is not a plateau, and the pattern says nothing about how long the interviews ran.

options.misconception: Reads a code as a measure of satisfaction.

options.text: How many codes each interviewee should learn to recognise in future.
options.misconception: Turns the analytic display into a teaching list.

questions.explanation: A joint display shows the distribution of codes across interviewees, which is where codes travel and where they stay put. It does not measure satisfaction, impose a coder ranking or produce a curriculum.
questions.hint: A display maps codes against people.

options.misconception: Treats repetition as independent evidence.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Chance-corrected agreement with lopsided margins
questions.learningObjective: Compute a corrected coefficient and contrast it with raw agreement.
questions.stem: Halvard Sten's two coders agree on 64 of 80 excerpts, and the chance-expected agreement from their code margins is 0.50.

options.text: The corrected coefficient is 0.60, well below the raw agreement of 0.80.
The corrected coefficient is 0.80, because chance agreement cancels out in the calculation.
options.misconception: Believes chance has no effect when expected agreement is given.

options.text: The corrected coefficient is 0.30, which is simply the gap between observed and expected.
options.misconception: Stops at the numerator of the correction.

options.text: The corrected coefficient is 0.20, because half the expected agreement must be removed.
options.misconception: Guesses a fraction instead of applying the formula.

questions.explanation: Observed agreement is 64 divided by 80, or 0.80, and the correction is (0.80 minus 0.50) over (1 minus 0.50), which is 0.30 over 0.50, giving 0.60. The raw figure flattered the coders.
questions.hint: Divide the gap by the headroom, not just take the gap.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: What a transferability claim rests on
questions.learningObjective: Describe what makes findings usable in an unfamiliar setting.
questions.stem: Anja Vogt wants her account of one branch's observing culture to be usable by a club she has never met.

answer.exemplar: The account should describe the branch's members, its setting, its routines and its constraints in enough detail that a distant reader can recognise which of those features are present in their own club and which are absent. It should also state plainly what the account does not claim, such as how far it travels in time or to observers with different equipment or routines. Transferability is a judgement the reader makes from a rich description, not a guarantee the author issues.

questions.explanation: Transferability is enabled by a rich description a reader can compare with their own setting, plus a clear statement of what is not claimed. A general statement of findings gives the reader nothing to compare.
questions.hint: Write for the reader who has to decide.

questions.topic: What a transferability claim rests on
questions.learningObjective: Write the boundary of a transferability claim alongside its content.
questions.stem: Bettina Kraus must write a paragraph explaining what her findings do and do not license other clubs to conclude.

answer.exemplar: The paragraph should distinguish two claims. It should say what the study found, tied to the branch, the period and the conditions actually studied, and it should say what remains undetermined, such as how the account would hold for observers with different routines, equipment or commitments. Readers need the boundary of the claim as much as its content, because a finding presented without its boundary invites application to cases the study never examined.

questions.explanation: A transferability claim needs both content and boundary: what was found, and the conditions it holds under. Reporting findings without their limits invites application to cases never studied.
questions.hint: Say what it covers and what it leaves open.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Extracts with no majority code
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the share of extracts carrying no majority code.
questions.stem: Ines Alvarado codes 80 extracts and finds that 10 of them have no code a second analyst would choose. What percentage of the coded extracts carry no majority code?
questions.explanation: Ten of the 80 coded extracts have no majority code, which is 10 divided by 80, or 12.5 percent. Reporting that share keeps the uncertainty visible instead of quietly reallocating those extracts.
questions.hint: Divide the ambiguous extracts by the coded extracts, then scale.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: New codes per interview after the plateau
questions.learningObjective: Select the justification for the number of interviews conducted.
questions.stem: Kit Marlowe is asked to justify the number of interviews he conducted and needs the right justification.

options.text: That the number of interviews equals the number of codes his study generated.
options.misconception: Invents a numerical rule for sample size.

options.text: That each code is represented by at least three interviews, which is why he stopped.
options.misconception: Uses a quota per code as the stopping rule.

options.text: That the codebook stopped changing under stated conditions, and he shows the pattern.
That a second analyst agreed with him on every final code, so no more were needed.
options.misconception: Uses agreement on final codes as the saturation evidence.

questions.explanation: Sample size is justified by the codebook stopping under stated conditions, with the pattern shown so a reader can check it. Counting codes, quotas per code and a second coder's agreement are all numbers without a rationale behind them.
questions.hint: Justify the size with something observable.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Coverage of a joint display
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the density of a joint display.
questions.stem: Mei-Ling Chow's joint display has 9 codes and 10 interviewees, with 3 codes appearing for every interviewee.

options.text: Three codes for every interviewee means every participant raised everything on the list.
options.misconception: Equates a populated row with full coverage.

options.text: Three codes appear for every interviewee, filling 30 of the 90 cells.
Only the 30 filled cells matter, so the empty cells should be left out of the display.
options.misconception: Removes empty cells to make coverage look complete.

options.text: The density comes from a coding error, since no theme should reach every interviewee.
options.misconception: Treats wide coverage as suspicious rather than informative.

questions.explanation: Three codes filling all ten columns give 30 of the 90 possible cells, so coverage is real but partial. Empty cells still belong in the display, because they mark where the codes did not travel.
questions.hint: Multiply the codes that appear everywhere by the number of interviewees.

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Counting theme instances at the unit of analysis
questions.learningObjective: Phrase a claim about a theme at the correct unit of analysis.
questions.stem: Farida Boussaid's findings describe how often members spoke about a particular problem, and she wants to phrase the claim correctly.

options.text: She should count every time the problem was mentioned, since frequency shows importance.
options.misconception: Treats repetition as the measure of importance.

options.text: She should count the interviews in which the problem appears, since members are her unit.
She should count codes rather than members, since codes are the analytic building blocks.
options.misconception: Switches unit of analysis without saying so.

options.text: She should report both counts and say they answer the same question.
options.misconception: Claims two different units answer one question.

questions.explanation: The claim is about members, so the count that supports it is the number of interviews in which the problem appears. Frequency of mention, code counts and a mixed pair of figures all answer questions the study is not asking.
questions.hint: Name the unit, then count in it.
